Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Describe the etiologies of elbow stiffness.
Perform appropriate evaluation of patients with elbow stiffness.
Recognize the difference between intrinsic and extrinsic elbow contractures.
Review and select the appropriate treatment options and surgical approaches for patients with
debilitating elbow contractures.
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
Standard activities of daily living require 100° (30° to 130°) of flexion/extension and 100°
(50°/50°) of pronation/supination.



More contemporary tasks (eg, cell phone and mouse/computer work) require more flexion
range of motion (ROM).

Overview
The elbow is a highly constrained joint that is predisposed to elbow stiffness to varying
degrees (Resource 1). A functional arc of motion is defined as the amount of elbow
extension and flexion required to perform most activities of daily living and has
historically been considered from 30° shy of full extension to 130° of flexion.1 As society
has evolved, many patients desire more ROM to complete daily tasks, such as requiring
142° of flexion to use a cell phone, 65° of pronation to use a keyboard, and 77° of
supination to open a door.2
Epidemiology
Elbow stiffness often is associated with arthritis or trauma (dislocations and/or fractures).
Other causes
Congenital: arthrogryposis, radial head dislocation
Cerebral palsy
Head injury: risk of heterotopic ossification
A burn that results in contracted skin eschar or heterotopic ossification

Epidemiology
Several conditions have been linked to elbow stiffness. Specifically, degenerative and
posttraumatic conditions have been associated with arthrofibrosis. Limited elbow ROM
may be observed with several congenital and genetic conditions, such as arthrogryposis
and a congenital radial head dislocation. In addition, heterotopic ossification is
commonly observed in patients with elbow stiffness and has been linked to acute elbow
injuries (Resource 1). Heterotopic ossification has been reported to occur in 3% of
patients with a simple elbow-dislocation, 20% of patients with a periarticular fracture-
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:04 PM
AAOS | Elbow Stiffness
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000040
2/24

dislocation, and as many as 75% to 89% of patients with elbow injuries associated with
head trauma.3
Anatomy and Biomechanics
The elbow joint is highly congruent and constrained.
The elbow consists of the ulnohumeral, radiocapitellar, and proximal radioulnar articulations.
All the articulations are encased by a contiguous joint capsule, in close proximity to the elbow
ligaments.

Anatomy and Biomechanics
The elbow joint consists of three articulations that are contained within a single synovial
cavity, which is in close proximity to the joint capsule, ligaments, and forearm
musculature (Resource 1). The inherent stability provided by the bony architecture,
combined with a thin capsule, typically allows for stable full ROM in the uninjured setting
(Figures 1 and 2).

Etiology
Several theories exist with regard to the etiology of elbow contracture.
Soft-tissue thickening has been evaluated in animal studies, which demonstrate:
Increased transforming growth factor-ß1
Decreased type III collagen
Increased myofibroblast activity
Increased extracellular matrix proliferation
Increased formation of collagen cross-links
Development of heterotopic ossification
Mature lamellar bone in atypical locations
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:04 PM
AAOS | Elbow Stiffness
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000040
5/24

Leads to loss of motion in:
Flexion/extension plane
Supination/pronation plane

Etiology
The cause of elbow stiffness can be subdivided into causes that are inherent to the
integrity of the articular surface or osseous structures (intrinsic) or causes that are
related to the surrounding structures, namely soft tissue (extrinsic). Often, a
combination of factors leads to a cascade of events limiting motion in the elbow.
Specifically, trauma and posttraumatic disorders are associated with a high propensity
for soft-tissue arthrofibrosis (Resource 2). In these settings, multiple molecular changes
have been identified, including expression of transforming growth factor-ß1 leading to a
decrease in type III collage and an increase in myofibroblast activity, which play a role in
the development of capsular thickening.4 In addition, heterotopic ossification is the
formation of mature lamellar bone in areas without bone, typically, leading to a loss of
motion.
Classification
Contractures can be classified as intrinsic, extrinsic, or mixed-type.
Intrinsic contracture (intra-articular)
Intra-articular fracture malunion
Joint incongruity
Inflammatory arthropathy
Osteochondritis dissecans
Posttraumatic arthritis
Osteoarthritis
Loss of articular cartilage
Marginal osteophytes
Extrinsic contracture (extra-articular)
Heterotopic ossification
Skin eschar
SEND FEEDBACK

6/24

Burn
Myositis ossificans
Capsular contracture
Mixed contracture
Late sequelae of intrinsic contracture

Classification
Elbow stiffness and contractures are classified (Table 1) based on the underlying
condition that is causing the contracture. An intra-articular cause is classified as an
intrinsic contracture and often is related to an osseous problem. An extra-articular cause
is classified as an extrinsic contracture and often is related to a soft-tissue contracture. A
contracture in a patient with intra-articular and extra-articular pathology is classified as
mixed. The latter is the most common form of contracture and commonly is observed in
patients with posttraumatic contractures.


Patient History
The first step in the workup of a patient with an elbow contracture is a thorough history.
This should include an assessment of the inciting event; if trauma occurred; the severity
of the trauma; the treatment performed and the duration of immobilization; any surgical
treatment; and any prior nonsurgical treatment options, including dynamic splinting,
therapy, and injections. More importantly, the effect of the contracture on the patient’s
SEND FEEDBACK

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000040
8/24

activities of daily living is of paramount importance in order to guide treatment decision
making (Resource 3).
Physical Examination
Complete hand, wrist, shoulder assessment
Elbow soft-tissue evaluation
Prior skin incisions
Evidence of infection
Eschar
Elbow ROM
Active and passive motion
Flexion
Extension
Supination
Pronation
Contralateral ROM for comparison
Pain
Terminal end-arc pain
Mid-arc pain
Neurovascular examination
Ulnar nerve evaluation
Presence of subluxation
Evidence of ulnar nerve transposition
Sensory and motor examination

Physical Examination
A complete physical examination is imperative in evaluating patients with an elbow
contracture (Resource 3). The integrity of the soft tissue needs to be assessed. All prior
skin incisions need to be assessed because this will help guide future management. In
addition, eschar formation and/or evidence of infection will help delineate the etiology of
the contracture, which ultimately guides management. In assessing ROM, assessment of
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:04 PM
AAOS | Elbow Stiffness
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000040
9/24

both extremities for comparison is essential. A complete assessment of active and
passive ROM measured with the use of a goniometer for accuracy allows the provider to
quantify the severity of the contracture (Resource 4). In addition, the quality of the end
point on passive testing will help assess the contracture. For example, a firm end point is
indicative of an osseous block to motion and likely an intrinsic contracture, whereas a
soft end point is indicative of a soft-tissue contracture and an extrinsic contracture. Pain
on ROM also helps determine treatment options. Pain at the terminal end-arc of ROM is
related to the contracture and likely will improve with resolution of the contracture.
Conversely, pain at the mid-arc of ROM occurs with intra-articular pathology and is
unlikely to improve with resolution of the contracture.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Always necessary
AP, lateral, and oblique radiographs are standard.
Serial radiographs to assess maturity of heterotopic ossification
Computed Tomography
Assess osteophyte and/or loose body pattern
Assess malunion
Assess heterotopic ossification location and maturity
Asses articular integrity
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
Rarely indicated

Imaging Studies
Imaging studies are a crucial component of the complete assessment for patients with
elbow contractures. The primary imaging modality is standard radiography of the elbow.

A radiocapitellar view as well as AP, lateral, and oblique radiographs can be obtained.
Evidence of prior surgical management, prior implants, evidence of degenerative
changes, osteophyte formation, and heterotopic ossification can be observed. Serial
radiographs are useful in patients with heterotopic ossification to determine if the
lamellar bone is mature (Figure 3). CT is not useful in patients with an isolated extrinsic
contracture who do not have heterotopic ossification (Figure 4). In other patients, it may
be a useful adjunct for surgical planning, allowing for assessment of osteophyte
patterns, loose body locations, severity of malunion, and articular integrity to guide
patient expectations, and to determine the location and maturity of heterotopic
ossification. Three-dimensional CT reconstruction is helpful to visually assess these
findings.
Figure 3 Lateral radiographs of a right elbow. A, Radiograph obtained 4 weeks after
trauma demonstrates the typical appearance of heterotopic ossification as a fluffy, ill-
defined density. B, Radiograph obtained 8 weeks after trauma demonstrates
consolidation of the ectopic bone with poorly defined borders. C, Radiograph obtained
16 weeks after trauma demonstrates a mature ossification with sharp cortical margins.

Electromyography

Management
The goals of treatment in patients with elbow stiffness are threefold:
1. Maintain and achieve functional ROM for the patient's desired activities of daily living.
2. Maintain painless ROM.
3. Maintain elbow stability.
Nonsurgical Management
Techniques/Procedures
Supervised physical therapy
NSAIDs and intra-articular corticosteroid injections
Splinting/ROM regimen
Dynamic splinting
Static progressive splinting or turnbuckle orthosis (adjustable static type)
Serial cast immobilization
Joint manipulation under anesthesia

Nonsurgical Management
Nonsurgical management of elbow stiffness is a reasonable treatment option for
patients with posttraumatic contractures, specifically if initiated early after the
development of a contracture (Figure 5). Dynamic splinting and static progressive
splinting are associated with equivalent results. However, patients should be counseled
that many as 6 to 12 months may be required to achieve optimal results. This requires
patient and physician patience.5

Surgical Management—Contracture Release
Indications
Extrinsic contracture
Mature heterotopic ossification
Intrinsic contracture with congruent articulation
Mixed contracture
Flexion contracture of 30°
Less than 120° of flexion
Patient willing to comply with rehabilitation protocol

Indications
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:04 PM
AAOS | Elbow Stiffness
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000040
14/24

Typically, indications for surgical treatment include patients with extrinsic, intrinsic, or
mixed contractures in whom a course of nonsurgical treatment fails (Resource 1). Most
surgeons agree that ROM parameters indicative of a surgical procedure are a flexion
contracture of 30° or less than 120° of flexion. Some patients may require additional
ROM for athletic activities or occupational demands. Patients in whom surgical release is
indicated must be able and willing to comply with a comprehensive rehabilitation
regimen.
Contraindications
Intra-articular ankylosed elbow
Neurologic elbow disorder
Charcot elbow
A deficient skin envelope (may need a rotational flap)
Immature heterotopic ossification
Incongruous ulnohumeral articulation
Posttraumatic arthritis

Contraindications
Several contraindications to contracture release exist. In patients with an osseous block
to motion from heterotopic ossification, observation of maturation of bone and stability
on serial radiographs and well-corticated margins are important. In addition, incongruity
of the elbow joint and degenerative changes are contraindications to a contracture
release because the procedure is unlikely to yield substantial gain in ROM and likely will
exacerbating pain.
Techniques/Procedures
Arthroscopic Capsular Release/Osteocapsular Arthroplasty
Anesthesia

Patient positioning
Can be performed in the lateral or prone position
Procedure
Anterior compartment
Posterior compartment
Ulnar nerve

Arthroscopic Capsular Release/Osteocapsular Arthroplasty
Arthroscopic contracture release is an effective procedure that requires a high degree of
skill and experience (Resource 5). It is indicated for osteoarthritis and extrinsic
contractures in patients with preserved joint congruity. Careful consideration must be
given to protecting neurovascular structures via the use of surface landmarks, the
careful use of retractors and accessory portals, and the judicial use of cautery and
shavers (Figure 6). Prior ulnar nerve transposition may be considered a relative
contraindication to an arthroscopic decompression.

Figure 6 Intraoperative photographs of a left elbow. A, Superficial anatomy of the medial
aspect of the elbow. The ulnar nerve (UN) is traced. B, Superficial anatomy of the lateral
aspect of the elbow. DPP = direct posterior portal, LE = lateral epicondyle, ME = medial

which is helpful for placement of retractors to improve visualization. (Reproduced from
Keener JD, Galatz LM: Arthroscopic management of the stiff elbow. J Am Acad Orthop Surg
2011;19[5]:265-274.)
The procedure is divided into management of the anterior and posterior compartments.
In anterior compartment, surgeons may address oteophytes of the coronoid and the
radial fossae, address the coronoid tip, and remove loose bodies. In addition, an anterior
capsulotomy or capsulectomy may be performed to improve elbow extension. Because
of the proximity of the radial nerve and the median nerve along the anterior capsule,
this should be performed carefully. In posterior compartment, surgeons may address
osteophytes of the olecranon fossa, address the olecranon tip, and remove loose bodies.
In addition, the posterior capsule is released. Care is taken along the posteromedial
gutter to avoid injury to the ulnar nerve.

The posterior bundle of the medial ulnar collateral ligament may limit elbow flexion and
may require a concomitant open procedure to improve ROM. In patients with less than
90°, prophylactic ulnar nerve decompression is indicated (Resource 5).
Open Surgical Contracture Release
Anesthesia
Surgery can be performed with general and regional, regional alone, or general alone.
Patient positioning
Typically performed in the supine position
Procedure
Approaches
Lateral column approach
Medial over-the-top approach
Combined approach

Open Surgical Contracture Release
Open surgical contracture release can be performed via a lateral, medial, or combined
approach (Resource 6). The latter commonly is used in patient with a severe elbow
contracture greater than 90° to allow for release of common lateral pathology and
decompression of the ulnar nerve and for release of the posterior bundle of the medial
ulnar collateral ligament. 
With the lateral column approach,6 the typical Kocher interval is developed and
extended proximally along the posterior supracondylar ridge, allowing the triceps and
the anconeus muscle to be elevated. This exposes the posterior capsule and the
posterior compartment structures. Next, the anterior plane is developed between the
extensor carpi radialis longus and the extensor carpi radialis brevis, allowing the
extensor carpi radialis longus and the brachialis muscle to be elevated carefully off the
anterior capsule, which typically is very thickened. Intra-articular visualization of the
coronoid, the radial fossae, and the coronoid tip should be clear from lateral to medial,
allowing for complete and thorough débridement (Figure 7).
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:04 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000040

The medial approach typically is reserved for isolated, medially located heterotopic
ossification or patients with medial hardware. During the procedure, the ulnar nerve is
transposed anteriorly, and the triceps is lifted from the intermuscular septum, exposing
the posterior compartment for capsular release, medial ulnar collateral ligament release,
and management of osteophytes along the olecranon fossa and the olecranon tip. In
addition, the flexor-pronator mass is incised and reflected from the medial epicondyle,
elevating the muscle from the anterior capsule to allow for visualization of the coronoid
and radial fossae and coronoid débridement (Figure 7).
The procedure can be performed through a standard utilitarian posterior incision or
through separate medial and/or lateral incisions.

elbow. A, Preoperative photograph shows the medial incision typically used for the deep
medial approach for release of the stiff elbow. B, The skin and subcutaneous tissue are
reflected, revealing the view of the entire flexor-pronator origin (arrowhead), medial
triceps (white arrow), and brachialis fascia (black arrow). C, The ulnar nerve is
decompressed and retracted anteriorly to allow for posterior joint exposure. The triceps

anteriorly. It is maintained in this position via the use of a fascial sling or by simply

Salvage Procedures
Interposition arthroplasty
Total elbow arthroplasty

Salvage Procedures
Patients with intrinsic contractures and joint incongruity typically require a salvage
procedure rather than primary arthroscopic or open contracture release. Treatment is
based on patient age and activity level.
The ulnohumeral joint is resurfaced with the use of Achilles tendon allograft, dermal
allograft, xenograft, autologous fascia lata, or other material. Outcomes rely on
maintained elbow stability. Typically, a hinged external fixator is used to maintain
stability while allowing motion.7 Interposition arthroplasty typically indicated is in
relatively young patients with articular damage and limited elbow ROM.8
Total elbow arthroplasty is reserved for elderly and low-demand patients with intrinsic
elbow contractures and degenerative changes given the high failure rate in younger and
active patients.
Postoperative Care
Rehabilitation
Continuous passive motion
Supervised physical therapy
Active and active-assisted ROM
Edema control
SEND FEEDBACK

20/24

Splinting

Postoperative Care
The efficacy of continuous passive motion in the management of elbow contractures and
in the postoperative rehabilitation protocol has not been definitively determined in the
literature.9 Regardless, supervised physical and/or occupational therapy, with early
active and active-assisted ROM exercises, edema control with compressive stockings,
and splinting for as long as 6 months postoperatively, is important for optimal function.
Complications
Heterotopic ossification or recurrent contracture
Nerve injury
Seroma
Wound problems

Complications
Prophylaxis for heterotopic ossification often is recommended after arthroscopic or
open contracture release. Typically, indomethacin (or other NSAID) can be used, or
prophylactic radiation therapy with 600 to 700 cGy is indicated.
Ulnar nerve neuropraxia is common after elbow contracture release, specifically in
patents with limited preoperative flexion in whom the ulnar nerve has not been
decompressed.
